sentences.text: Although Eurotrochilus looks much like a modern hummingbird, it kept some ancient traits and is not closely related to any living species. This extinct genus represents the closest known relatives to the crown group Trochilidae, the family of modern hummingbirds.

Specimens are among the smallest fossil birds and belong to the order Apodiformes because of their shortened humeri and ulnae. The humeri measure between 6.0 and 6.5 millimeters and are considered short and stout compared to other Apodiformes, except extant hummingbirds.

Eurotrochilus possessed elongated beaks, a feature unknown in Jungornis, which serves as evidence of their ability to consume nectar. In some species, the skull and beak have been measured to be approximately 34 millimeters in length. The beaks are straight and narrow, measuring 15.5 to 20 millimeters in length, which is roughly 2.5 times the length of the cranium.

The widely separated maxillary processes in the palatine bones indicate that Eurotrochilus possessed rhynchokinesis, the ability to flex the upper beak. Large hyoid bones are thought to have supported a long, protractile tongue used for lapping up nectar.
Specializations in the humeri allowed the bone to rotate during hovering flight.
The genus Eurotrochilus was described by Gerald Mayr in 2004 after he found tiny skeletons in museum drawers.
Two species are currently recognized: E. inexpectatus described by Mayr in 2004 and E. noniewiczi described by Bochenski in 2007.

Fossils found in Germany, France, and Poland indicate that the Old World was the origin of the hummingbird family, despite all living species today being found in the New World. Eurotrochilus provided the strongest evidence that modern-looking hummingbirds existed in the Old World during the early Oligocene.

The species E. noniewiczi is named after Edward Noniewicza, the private collector who discovered the fossil specimen. The Polish specimen found at Winnica serves as the holotype for the new species Eurotrochilus noniewiczi.

Six specimens of Eurotrochilus have been found across Germany, France, and Poland. Dr. Antoine Louchart described a French specimen in 2007, which included an almost complete skeleton preserved on a slab.

Adaptations allowed it to consume nectar from ornithophilous flowers as its main nutrient source and to pollinate those flowers. Researchers suggest that Old World bird-pollinated flowers evolved their specific shapes in response to Eurotrochilus, which had long beaks, tongues, and hovering flight. The abundance of E. inexpectatus fossils suggests these birds were locally dominant pollinators of ornithophilous flowers in the early Oligocene.

The warm climate supported broad-leaved evergreen forests and palm-rich coastal forests where Eurotrochilus lived. Scientists believe Eurotrochilus experienced mild winters based on its fruit and nectar diet, though migration habits are unknown.
Eurotrochilus is an extinct genus of stem-group hummingbirds and represents the closest known relatives to the crown group Trochilidae.
Eurotrochilus lived during the Rupelian age of the Early Oligocene epoch within the Paleogene period. Eurotrochilus lived during the Rupelian age of the early Oligocene era.

Specimens of Eurotrochilus date to between 28 and 34 million years ago, with German fossils estimated at 32 million years old. Eurotrochilus lived between 33.9 and 27.3 million years ago during the Rupelian stage.
During the Oligocene, the Paratethys Ocean covered most of Central and Eastern Europe where Eurotrochilus fossils were found.

Recent estimates suggest Eurotrochilus lived between 28 and 34 million years ago, though the exact timing is debated. It is debated exactly when Eurotrochilus was present, with recent estimates suggesting a range of 28 to 34 million years ago.

It is debated whether competition with long-tongued bees caused the extinction of Eurotrochilus and European hummingbirds. Rapid climate change is another hypothesis for the extinction of Eurotrochilus, which would have been difficult for such a small bird to survive.
